text: The Seven Dials Mystery
by Agatha Christie
A Character Echo Production
Chapter I

On Early Rising. That amiable youth, Jimmy Thesiger, came racing down the big staircase at Chimneys two steps at a time. So precipitate was his descent that he collided with Tredwell, the stately butler, just as the latter was crossing the hall bearing a fresh supply of hot coffee. Owing to the marvellous presence of mind and masterly agility of Tredwell, no casualty occurred.
Sorry. I say, Tredwell, am I the last down?
No, sir, Mr. Wade has not come down yet.
Good.

Jimmy entered the breakfast-room. The room was empty save for his hostess, and her reproachful gaze gave Jimmy the same feeling of discomfort he always experienced on catching the eye of a defunct codfish exposed on a fishmonger's slab.
Afraid I'm a bit late, Lady Coote. What?
Oh! it doesn't matter.

She sighed now, heavily, and drifted out through the open window. Lady Coote stood for a few moments tragically on the terrace and then nerved herself to speak to MacDonald, the head gardener, who was surveying the domain over which he ruled with an autocratic eye. Lady Coote approached him nervously.
Good-morning, MacDonald.
Good-morning, m'lady.
I was wondering—could we have some of those late grapes for dessert to-night?
They're no fit for picking yet.
Oh. Oh! but I was in the end house yesterday, and I tasted one and they seemed very good.
If you had given orders, m'lady, a bunch should have been cut and sent in to you.
Oh, thank you. Yes, I will do that another time.
But they're no properly fit for picking yet.

No. No, I suppose not. We'd better leave it then. I was going to speak to you about the piece of lawn at the back of the rose garden. I wondered if it could be used as a bowling green. Sir Oswald is very fond of a game of bowls.
Nae doot it could be used for that purpose.
If it was cleared up and—er—cut—and—er—all that sort of thing.
Aye. It could be done. But it would mean taking William from the lower border.
Oh!
And that would be a pity.
Oh! of course. It would.
Of course, if it's your orders, m'lady—
Oh! no. I see what you mean, MacDonald. N-no—William had better get on with the lower border.
That's what I thocht meself, m'lady.
Yes. Yes. Certainly.
I thocht you'd gree, m'lady.
Oh! certainly.
MacDonald touched his hat and moved away. Lady Coote sighed unhappily and looked after him. Jimmy Thesiger, replete with kidneys and bacon, stepped out on to the terrace beside her.
Topping morning, eh?
Is it? Oh! yes, I suppose it is. I hadn't noticed.
Where are the others? Punting on the lake?
I expect so. I mean, I shouldn't wonder if they were.
Lady Coote turned and plunged abruptly into the house again. Tredwell was just examining the coffee pot.
Oh, dear. Isn't Mr.—Mr.—
Wade, m'lady?
Yes, Mr. Wade. Isn't he down yet?
No, m'lady.
It's very late.
Yes, m'lady.
Oh! dear. I suppose he will come down sometime, Tredwell?
Oh, undoubtedly, m'lady. It was eleven thirty yesterday morning when Mr. Wade came down, m'lady.
It's very hard luck on you, Tredwell. Having to clear and then get lunch on the table by one o'clock.
I am accustomed to the ways of young gentlemen, m'lady.
Lady Coote blushed for the second time that morning. But a welcome interruption occurred. The door opened and a serious, spectacled young man put his head in.
Oh! there you are, Lady Coote. Sir Oswald was asking for you.
Oh, I'll go to him at once, Mr. Bateman.
Lady Coote hurried out. Rupert Bateman, who was Sir Oswald's private secretary, went out the other way, through the window where Jimmy Thesiger was still lounging amiably.
Morning, Pongo. I suppose I shall have to go and make myself agreeable to those blasted girls. You coming?
Bateman shook his head and hurried along the terrace and in at the library window. Jimmy grinned pleasantly at his retreating back.
Jimmy yawned and strolled slowly down to the lake. The girls were there, three of them, with his two friends, Bill Eversleigh and Ronny Devereux.
Hallo, said Nancy, or possibly Helen.
It's Jimmy. Where's what's his name?
You don't mean to say that Gerry Wade's not up yet? Something ought to be done about it.
If he's not careful he'll miss his breakfast altogether one day—find it's lunch or tea instead when he rolls down.
It's a shame. Because it worries Lady Coote so. She gets more and more like a hen that wants to lay an egg and can't. It's too bad.
Let's pull him out of bed. Come on, Jimmy.
Oh! let's be more subtle than that.
I'm not subtle. I don't know how.

Let's get together and do something about it to-morrow morning. You know, get him up at seven. Stagger the household. Tredwell loses his false whiskers and drops the tea urn. Lady Coote has hysterics and faints in Bill's arms—Bill being the weight carrier. Sir Oswald says 'Ha!' and steel goes up a point and five eighths. Pongo registers emotion by throwing down his spectacles and stamping on them.
You don't know Gerry. I daresay enough cold water might wake him—judiciously applied, that is. But he'd only turn over and go to sleep again.
Oh! we must think of something more subtle than cold water.
Well, what?
We ought to be able to think of something. Who's got any brains?
Pongo. And here he is, rushing along in a hurried manner as usual. Pongo was always the one for brains. It's been his misfortune from his youth upwards. Let's turn Pongo on to it.
Mr. Bateman listened patiently to a somewhat incoherent statement. His attitude was that of one poised for flight. He delivered his solution without loss of time.
I should suggest an alarum clock. I always use one myself for fear of oversleeping. I find that early tea brought in in a noiseless manner is sometimes powerless to awaken one.
He hurried away.
An alarum clock. One alarum clock. It would take about a dozen to disturb Gerry Wade.
Well, why not? I've got it. Let's all go into Market Basing and buy an alarum clock each.
There was laughter and discussion. Bill and Ronny went off to get hold of cars. Jimmy was deputed to spy upon the dining-room. He returned rapidly.
He's there right enough. Making up for lost time and wolfing down toast and marmalade. How are we going to prevent him coming along with us?
It was decided that Lady Coote must be approached and instructed to hold him in play. Jimmy and Nancy and Helen fulfilled this duty. Lady Coote was bewildered and apprehensive.

A rag? You will be careful, won't you, my dears? I mean, you won't smash the furniture and wreck things or use too much water. We've got to hand this house over next week, you know. I shouldn't like Lord Caterham to think—

That's all right, Lady Coote. Bundle Brent—Lord Caterham's daughter—is a great friend of mine. And there's nothing she'd stick at—absolutely nothing! You can take it from me. And anyway there's not going to be any damage done. This is quite a quiet affair.
Subtle.
Lady Coote went sadly along the terrace just as Gerald Wade emerged from the breakfast-room.
Morning, Lady Coote. Where are all the others?
They've all gone to Market Basing.
What for?
Some joke.
Rather early in the morning for jokes.
It's not so very early in the morning.
I'm afraid I was a bit late coming down. It's an extraordinary thing, but wherever I happen to be staying, I'm always last to be down.
Very extraordinary.
I don't know why it is. I can't think, I'm sure.
Why don't you just get up?
Oh!
I've heard Sir Oswald say so many times that there's nothing for getting a young man on in the world like punctual habits.

Oh! I know. And I have to when I'm in town. I mean, I have to be round at the jolly old Foreign Office by eleven o'clock. You mustn't think I'm always a slacker, Lady Coote. I say, what awfully jolly flowers you've got down in that lower border. I can't remember the names of them, but we've got some at home—those mauve thingummybobs. My sister's tremendously keen on gardening.
What kind of gardeners do you have?
Oh! just one. Rather an old fool, I believe. Doesn't know much, but he does what he's told. And that's a great thing, isn't it?
Meanwhile the expedition was doing well. The principal emporium of Market Basing had been invaded and the sudden demand for alarum clocks was considerably puzzling the proprietor.
I wish we'd got Bundle here. You know her, don't you, Jimmy? Oh, you'd like her. She's a splendid girl—a real good sport—and mark you, she's got brains too. You know her, Ronny?
Don't know Bundle? Where have you been vegetating? She's simply it.
Be a bit more subtle, Bill. Stop blethering about your lady friends and get on with the business.

If you'll allow me to advise you, Miss, I should say—not the 7/11 one. It's a good clock—I'm not running it down, mark you, but I should strongly advise this kind at 10/6. Well worth the extra money. Reliability, you understand. I shouldn't like you to say afterwards—
We don't want a reliable clock.
It's got to go for one day, that's all.
We don't want a subtle one. We want one with a good loud ring.
We want—

Bill was unable to finish, because Jimmy, who was of a mechanical turn of mind, had at last grasped the mechanism. For the next five minutes the shop was hideous with the loud raucous ringing of many alarum clocks. In the end six excellent starters were selected.
And I'll tell you what. I'll get one for Pongo. It was his idea, and it's a shame that he should be out of it. He shall be represented among those present.
That's right. And I'll take an extra one for Lady Coote. The more the merrier. And she's doing some of the spade work. Probably gassing away to old Gerry now.
The clocks were wrapped up and paid for. Mr. Murgatroyd watched the cars drive away with a puzzled air.
Chapter II
Concerning Alarum Clocks. Dinner was over. Lady Coote had been once more detailed for duty. Sir Oswald had unexpectedly come to the rescue by suggesting bridge.

The others were supposed to be dancing to the wireless in the big ballroom. In reality they were grouped around the door of Gerald Wade's bedroom, and the air was full of subdued giggles and the loud ticking of clocks.
Now where shall we put them?
Under the bed in a row? And what shall we set them at? What time, I mean? All together so that there's one glorious what-not, or at intervals?

The point was hotly disputed. One party argued that for a champion sleeper like Gerry Wade the combined ringing of eight alarum clocks was necessary. The other party argued in favour of steady and sustained effort. In the end the latter won the day. The clocks were set to go off one after the other, starting at 6:30 A.M.
And I hope that this will be a lesson to him.
Hear, hear.
The business of hiding the clocks was just being begun when there was a sudden alarm.
Hist. Somebody's coming up the stairs. It's all right. It's only Pongo.
Taking advantage of being dummy, Mr. Bateman was going to his room for a handkerchief. He paused on his way and took in the situation at a glance. He then made a comment, a simple and practical one.
He will hear them ticking when he goes to bed.
The conspirators looked at each other.
What did I tell you? Pongo always did have brains!
The brainy one passed on.
It's true. Eight clocks all ticking at once do make a devil of a row. Even old Gerry, ass as he is, couldn't miss it. He'll guess something's up.
I wonder if he is.
Is what?
Such an ass as we all think.
We all know old Gerald.
Do we? I've sometimes thought that—well, that it isn't possible for anyone to be quite the ass old Gerry makes himself out to be.
Jimmy, you've got brains.
A second Pongo.
Well, it just occurred to me, that's all.
Oh! don't let's all be subtle. What are we to do about these clocks?
Here's Pongo coming back again. Let's ask him.
Pongo, urged to bring his great brain to bear upon the matter, gave his decision.
Wait till he's gone to bed and got to sleep. Then enter the room very quietly and put the clocks down on the floor.
Little Pongo's right again. On the word one all park clocks, and then we'll go downstairs and disarm suspicion.
Bridge was still proceeding—with a slight difference. Sir Oswald was now playing with his wife.
I see, dear. It's so kind of you to tell me.
And she continued to make exactly the same errors. At intervals, Gerald Wade said to Pongo:
Well played, partner, jolly well played.

Say he goes to bed about twelve—what do you think we ought to give him—about an hour? Curious thing—three in the morning is my usual time for bye-bye, but to-night, just because I know we've got to sit up a bit, I'd give anything to be a mother's boy and turn in right away.
My dear Maria, I have told you over and over again not to hesitate when you are wondering whether to finesse or not. You give the whole table information.

Lady Coote smiled kindly, leaned her ample chest well forward over the table, and gazed firmly into Gerald Wade's hand where he sat on her right. Her anxieties lulled to rest by perceiving the queen, she played the knave and took the trick and proceeded to lay down her cards.
Four tricks and the rubber. I think I was very lucky to get four tricks there.
Lucky. Lucky, she calls it. That woman wants watching.
I know I'm not a good player. But I'm really very lucky at the game.
You'll never be a bridge player, Maria.
No, dear. I know I shan't. You're always telling me so. And I do try so hard.
She does. There's no subterfuge about it. She'd put her head right down on your shoulder if she couldn't see into your hand any other way.
I know you try. It's just that you haven't any card sense.
I know, dear. That's what you're always telling me. And you owe me another ten shillings, Oswald.
Do I?
Yes. Seventeen hundred—eight pounds ten. You've only given me eight pounds.
Dear me. My mistake.

Lady Coote smiled at him sadly and took up the extra ten-shilling note. Sir Oswald moved over to a side table and became hospitable with whisky and soda. It was half-past twelve when general good-nights were said.

Ronny Devereux, who had the room next door to Gerald Wade's, was told off to report progress. At a quarter to two he crept round tapping at doors. The party, pyjamaed and dressing-gowned, assembled with various scuffles and giggles and low whispers.
His light went out about twenty minutes ago. I thought he'd never put it out. I opened the door just now and peeped in, and he seems sound off. What about it?
Once more the clocks were solemnly assembled. Then another difficulty arose.
We can't all go barging in. Make no end of a row. One person's got to do it and the others can hand him the what-nots from the door.
Hot discussion then arose as to the proper person to be selected. In the end an overwhelming majority decided in favour of Rupert Bateman.

Pongo's the lad. Anyway, he walks like a cat—always did. And then, if Gerry should waken up, Pongo will be able to think of some rotten silly thing to say to him. You know, something plausible that'll calm him down and not rouse his suspicions.
Something subtle.
Exactly.

Pongo performed his job neatly and efficiently. Cautiously opening the bedroom door, he disappeared into the darkness inside bearing the two largest clocks. In a minute or two he reappeared on the threshold and two more were handed to him and then again twice more. Finally he emerged. Every one held his breath and listened. The rhythmical breathing of Gerald Wade could still be heard, but drowned, smothered and buried beneath the triumphant, impassioned ticking of Mr. Murgatroyd's eight alarum clocks.
Chapter III
Twelve o'clock.
The Joke That Failed. The joke—as a joke—had not gone off any too well. The alarum clocks, on the other hand, had performed their part.
The lad isn't human.
Probably thought he heard the telephone in the distance and rolled over and went to sleep again.
It seems to me very remarkable. I think he ought to see a doctor about it.
Some disease of the ear-drums.
Well, if you ask me, I think he's just spoofing us. Of course they woke him up. But he's just going to do us down by pretending that he didn't hear anything.
It's an idea.
He's subtle, that's what it is. You'll see, he'll be extra late for breakfast this morning—just to show us.

You forget, I was outside the door when the first one went off. Whatever old Gerry decided to do later, the first one must have surprised him. He'd have let out something about it. Where did you put it, Pongo?
On a little table close to his ear.
That was thoughtful of you, Pongo. Now, tell me. If a whacking great bell started ringing within a few inches of your ear at half-past six in the morning, what would you say about it?
Oh! Lord. I should say—

Of course you would. So should I. So would anyone. What they call the natural man would emerge. Well, it didn't. So I say that Pongo is right—as usual—and that Gerry has got an obscure disease of the ear-drums.
It's now twenty past twelve.
I say, that's a bit beyond anything, isn't it? I mean a joke's a joke. But this is carrying it a bit far. It's a shade hard on the Cootes.
What are you getting at?
Well, somehow or other—it's not like old Gerry.
It was at that moment Tredwell came into the room and looked round him hesitatingly.
I thought Mr. Bateman was here.
Just gone out this minute through the window. Can I do anything?
Tredwell's eyes wandered from him to Jimmy Thesiger and then back again. As though singled out, the two young men left the room with him. Tredwell closed the dining-room door carefully behind him.
Well. What's up?
Mr. Wade not having yet come down, sir, I took the liberty of sending Williams up to his room.
Yes.
Williams has just come running down in a great state of agitation, sir. I am afraid, sir, the poor young gentleman must have died in his sleep.
Nonsense. It's—it's impossible. Gerry—I'll—I'll run up and see. That fool Williams may have made a mistake.

No, sir, Williams has made no mistake. I have already sent for Dr. Cartwright, and in the meantime I have taken the liberty of locking the door, preparatory to informing Sir Oswald of what has occurred. I must now find Mr. Bateman.
Gerry.
Jimmy took his friend by the arm and pushed him down on to a seat.
Take it easy, old son. You'll get your wind in a minute. Poor old Gerry. If ever a man looked fit, he did.
Ronny nodded.
All that clock business seems so rotten now. It's odd, isn't it, why farce so often seems to get mixed up with tragedy?
I wish that doctor would come. I want to know—
Know what?
What he—died of.
Heart?
Ha!
I say, Ronny. You don't mean—you aren't thinking—I mean, you haven't got it into your head that—that, well, I mean he wasn't biffed on the head or anything? Tredwell's locking the door and all that.
It seemed to Jimmy that his words deserved an answer, but Ronny continued to stare straight out in front of him. Jimmy shook his head and relapsed into silence. It was Tredwell who disturbed them.
The doctor would like to see you two gentlemen in the library, if you please, sir.
Ronny sprang up. Jimmy followed him. Dr. Cartwright was a thin, energetic young man with a clever face. He greeted them with a brief nod.
I understand you were a great friend of Mr. Wade's.
His greatest friend.
H'm. Well, this business seems straightforward enough. Sad, though. He looked a healthy young chap. Do you know if he was in the habit of taking stuff to make him sleep?
Make him sleep? He always slept like a top.
You never heard him complain of sleeplessness?
Never.
Well, the facts are simple enough. There'll have to be an inquest, I'm afraid, nevertheless.
How did he die?
There's not much doubt; I should say an overdose of chloral. The stuff was by his bed. And a bottle and glass. Very sad, these things are.
There's no question of—foul play?
Why do you say that? Any cause to suspect it, eh?
No cause whatever.
And suicide—eh?
Certainly not.
No troubles that you know of? Money troubles? A woman?
Again Ronny shook his head.
Now about his relations. They must be notified.
He's got a sister—a half-sister rather. Lives at Deane Priory. About twenty miles from here. When he wasn't in town Gerry lived with her.
H'm. Well, she must be told.
I'll go. It's a rotten job, but somebody's got to do it. You know her, don't you?
Slightly. I've danced with her once or twice.
Then we'll go in your car. You don't mind, do you? I can't face it alone.
That's all right. I was going to suggest it myself. I'll go and get the old bus cranked up.

Presently the two friends were skimming along in Jimmy's car. They were silent till they reached Deane Priory. Miss Loraine, the maid told them, was in the garden. They went round into the somewhat neglected garden.
How do you do. You mustn't mind Elizabeth. She's just had some puppies and she's very suspicious.

She had a supremely natural manner and, as she looked up smiling, the faint wild rose flush deepened in her cheeks. Her eyes were a very dark blue—like cornflowers. Suddenly they widened—was it with alarm?
This is Ronny Devereux, Miss Wade. You must often have heard Gerry speak of him.
Oh! yes. You've both been staying at Chimneys, haven't you? Why didn't you bring Gerry over with you?
We—er—couldn't.
Miss Wade, I'm afraid—I mean, we've got bad news for you.
Gerry?
Yes—Gerry. He's—
Oh! tell me—tell me—You'll tell me.
Yes, Miss Wade, I'll tell you. Gerry is dead.
She had plenty of pluck. She gasped and drew back, but in a minute or two she was asking eager, searching questions. How? When? Ronny answered her as gently as he could.
Sleeping draught? Gerry?
The incredulity in her voice was plain. Jimmy gave her a glance. It was almost a glance of warning.
But I want to be—be alone a little first.
I know.
That's all right.
Thank you both ever so much for coming.
On returning to Chimneys Jimmy was waylaid by a tearful Lady Coote.
That poor boy. That poor boy.
Jimmy ran lightly up the stairs. Ronny was just emerging from Gerald Wade's room. He seemed taken aback at the sight of Jimmy.
I've been in to see him. Are you going in?
I don't think so.
I think all his friends ought to. Yes. It's a sign of respect.
Oh! very well.

Jimmy passed in, setting his teeth a little. There were white flowers arranged on the coverlet, and the room had been tidied and set to rights. As he turned to leave the room, his glance swept the mantelshelf and he stopped in astonishment. The alarum clocks had been ranged along it neatly in a row. He went out sharply. Ronny was waiting for him.
Looks very peaceful and all that. Rotten luck on him. I say, Ronny, who arranged all those clocks like that in a row?
How should I know? One of the servants, I suppose.
The funny thing is that there are seven of them, not eight. One of them's missing. Did you notice that?
Ronny made an inaudible sound.
Seven instead of eight. I wonder why.
